articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 million question: Where the tourist tax money actually goes
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending records shows more than half went to debt service on projects completed a decade ago.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.3 million in tourist development taxes in fiscal year 2025, the highest total in county history.

More than $25 million—roughly 54 percent—went to debt service payments on bonds issued for projects including the Bay Center renovation and Pensacola Beach infrastructure completed between 2012 and 2016.
Visit Pensacola received $8.2 million for marketing and operations, while direct beach maintenance and public amenities received less than $4 million combined.
articles.body:
The receipt arrives every night at hotels and vacation rentals across Escambia County. Five percent added to the room rate. A family paying $200 a night for a gulf-front condo contributes $10 to what Florida law calls the tourist development tax. Locals call it the bed tax.

Last fiscal year, those nickels and dimes added up to $47.3 million—a record for the county and a 12 percent increase over the previous year. But a Flightline review of Tourist Development Council expenditure reports, bond documents and county budget records reveals that the largest share of that money never touches a beach umbrella or funds a new festival. It goes to banks.

Debt service consumed $25.6 million of the fiscal year 2025 bed tax revenue. That's 54 percent of the total, paid toward bonds issued more than a decade ago for projects that have long since opened their doors.

The bonds that keep on billing

The biggest obligation traces to 2012. That year, the county issued $93 million in tourist development revenue bonds to renovate the Pensacola Bay Center and fund infrastructure improvements on Pensacola Beach. The Bay Center got new seats, upgraded concourses and modernized mechanical systems. The beach got repaved roads, improved stormwater drainage and renovated public restrooms at Casino Beach.

Fourteen years later, the county still owes $67.4 million on those bonds. Annual payments run approximately $8.9 million through 2037.

A second bond issue in 2015 added another $41 million to the ledger, funding construction of the Pensacola Beach Gulf Pier replacement and additional Bay Center improvements. That debt carries through 2040 with annual payments averaging $4.2 million.

County records show three additional smaller bond issues between 2016 and 2019 totaling $38 million for various beach projects and tourism facility maintenance. Combined annual debt service on all outstanding tourist development bonds reached $25.6 million last fiscal year.

"The math is the math," said County Administrator Wes Moreno during a budget workshop in May. "We made commitments. We honor them."

What's left over

After debt service, the next largest expenditure category is marketing. Visit Pensacola, the county's destination marketing organization, received $8.2 million in fiscal year 2025. That funded advertising campaigns in Atlanta, Nashville, Birmingham and Dallas. It paid for travel writer visits and social media content creation. It covered salaries for 23 full-time employees and office space in downtown Pensacola.

Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer defended the spending in an interview. "Every dollar we put into marketing returns $7 in visitor spending," he said, citing a study commissioned by the organization in 2024. "That's not my number. That's Tourism Economics."

The study, conducted by the Oxford Economics subsidiary, relied on visitor survey data and modeling. Independent verification of the $7 return figure is not possible from public records.

Below marketing on the expenditure list: $3.8 million for beach maintenance and public amenities. That category covers lifeguard operations, beach trash collection, restroom maintenance and the seasonal trolley service. It represents 8 percent of total collections.

Grants to local events and cultural organizations totaled $2.1 million. Recipients included the Pensacola Crawfish Festival, Gallery Night, the Pensacola Symphony Orchestra and the Pensacola Little Theatre. Individual grants ranged from $5,000 to $175,000.

The remaining $7.6 million went to administrative costs, reserves and a transfer to the county general fund for tourism-related code enforcement.

The statutory framework

Florida law restricts how tourist development tax revenue can be spent. The money must promote tourism or fund tourism-related facilities. Counties cannot redirect bed tax dollars to schools, roads or public safety—even during budget shortfalls.

But within those restrictions, local governments have broad discretion. Some Florida counties direct larger percentages toward beach renourishment or public access improvements. Others prioritize convention center expansion or sports facility construction.

Escambia County's allocation reflects decisions made primarily between 2010 and 2015, when commissioners approved the major bond issues. Those decisions locked in spending patterns for decades.

"We're paying for our parents' choices," said Commissioner Jeff Bergosh at a June Tourist Development Council meeting. Bergosh was elected in 2012, the same year the largest bond issue closed. He voted against the Bay Center renovation as a member of the Escambia County School Board but had no vote on the county commission at the time.

Competing priorities

Not everyone agrees the current allocation serves residents or tourists well. At the June TDC meeting, public comment included complaints about overcrowded beach parking, inadequate public restroom facilities and the lack of shade structures at Casino Beach.

Maria Santos, who identified herself as a property manager for 34 vacation rental units on Pensacola Beach, told the council that her guests consistently complain about beach access. "They're paying the tax," she said. "They should see the benefit."

TDC member and hotelier Robert Rinke pushed back on suggestions that debt service represents wasted money. "The Bay Center brings people here," he said. "Concerts, hockey games, conventions. Those heads in beds didn't exist before the renovation."

The Bay Center hosted 127 events in fiscal year 2025, according to SMG, the facility's management company. Total attendance was 412,000. How many of those attendees stayed overnight in paid accommodations is not tracked.

Looking ahead

Some relief is on the horizon. The 2012 bonds will be fully retired in 2037. The 2015 bonds follow in 2040. Assuming no new major debt issuances, annual debt service obligations will drop below $10 million by 2038.

But commissioners are already discussing new projects. A proposed Pensacola Beach welcome center has an estimated cost of $12 million. Expansion of the Gulf Islands National Seashore parking area—if the county contributes a local match—could require $8 million. A convention center hotel, long discussed and never built, remains on some commissioners' wish lists.

Each project would likely require new bonds. Each new bond issue would extend the cycle.

For now, the tourist dollars keep flowing in. And more than half keep flowing out to creditors.

The next Tourist Development Council meeting is scheduled for August 14 at the Escambia County Central Office Complex. Public comment periods are held at the beginning and end of each meeting.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The last trailer park on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Camp Gulf has survived hurricanes, buyout offers, and rising insurance costs for 60 years. Its residents say this summer feels different.
brief: Camp Gulf, established in 1966, remains the only trailer park on Pensacola Beach with 47 occupied lots on Santa Rosa Island
Residents face insurance costs that have tripled since 2020 and mounting pressure from developers offering buyouts
A proposed Escambia County lease renegotiation this fall could determine the park's future on the barrier island
articles.body:
The wind sock above Lot 23 hangs limp in the July heat. Beneath it, 74-year-old Don Rafferty sits in a lawn chair bolted to a concrete pad, watching the afternoon storm clouds build over the Gulf of Mexico. His single-wide has occupied this spot for 31 years. The nameplate above the door still reads "Rafferty" in faded gold letters.

"Every summer I think it might be the last one," Rafferty said. "This summer I actually believe it."

Camp Gulf is the last trailer park on Pensacola Beach. The 3.2-acre property sits on the southern edge of Santa Rosa Island, wedged between a Holiday Inn Express and a stretch of undeveloped dune. Forty-seven trailers occupy lots arranged in tight rows, some with wooden decks and window boxes, others showing the rust and wear of decades in salt air.

The park opened in 1966, back when Pensacola Beach was a summer destination for middle-class families from Alabama and Mississippi, not a real estate market where beachfront lots sell for $2 million. For 60 years it has survived hurricanes Ivan, Dennis, Sally, and a half-dozen unnamed storms. It has survived three ownership changes and at least five serious buyout offers from hotel developers.

What it may not survive is the economics of 2026.

The math doesn't work

Lot rent at Camp Gulf runs $875 per month, which includes water and sewer. That figure has increased 40% since 2020. But lot rent is not what keeps residents awake at night.

Insurance is.

Rafferty paid $1,100 annually to insure his trailer in 2019. His current policy costs $4,200. He is among the lucky ones. Seven residents told The Flightline they cannot obtain private insurance at any price and now rely on Citizens Property Insurance, Florida's insurer of last resort. Citizens policies for mobile homes in flood zones start at $5,500 annually.

"I'm on Social Security," said Marie Odom, 68, who has lived at Camp Gulf since 2003. "My lot rent and insurance together cost more than my check. I make up the difference with what my husband left me. That money runs out in maybe two years."

Odom's trailer, a 2001 Fleetwood, is worth approximately $15,000 according to NADA guides. She pays $6,100 per year to insure it.

Camp Gulf owner Gerald "Jerry" Hutchins declined multiple interview requests for this story. Through his attorney, he provided a written statement: "Camp Gulf continues to operate as it has for six decades. We comply with all Escambia County lease requirements and maintain the property to required standards."

Pressure from all sides

The land beneath Camp Gulf belongs to Escambia County. Like most of Pensacola Beach, it sits on a long-term lease from the Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages development on the barrier island. Hutchins holds a commercial sublease that expires in 2048.

But the lease comes up for renegotiation every five years. The next review is scheduled for October.

Escambia County Commission Chair Jeff Bergosh said in a June meeting that the county has received "significant interest" from developers regarding the Camp Gulf parcel. He did not name the developers or specify what kind of development they proposed.

"The commission's obligation is to maximize value for taxpayers while respecting existing lease agreements," Bergosh said. "Those two things aren't always compatible."

Santa Rosa Island Authority records show the Camp Gulf lease generates $67,000 annually for the county. A 2024 appraisal valued the land at $8.4 million for hotel development. A hotel of comparable size to adjacent properties would generate an estimated $340,000 in annual lease payments.

Residents say they've seen the same appraisers and surveyors on the property three times since January.

"They don't talk to us," said Wayne Poole, 61, a retired electrician who bought his trailer in 2018. "They just walk around with clipboards and take pictures. What are we supposed to think?"

What remains

On a Wednesday afternoon, Camp Gulf feels less like a place under siege than a small town going about its business. A woman in Lot 8 tends tomato plants in five-gallon buckets. Two men in Lot 31 drink Busch Light and argue about the Pensacola Blue Wahoos' bullpen. Someone's wind chimes play a melody that sounds almost deliberate.

The trailers themselves range from the well-maintained to the barely habitable. Several sport fresh paint and new awnings. Others have plywood over windows and tarps over sections of roof. One near the back of the property appears abandoned, its door hanging open and palmetto fronds growing through the decking.

Hutchins' statement noted that four trailers were removed in the past year for lease violations, and that occupancy has declined from 52 lots to 47 since 2023.

Residents offer different explanations. Some say neighbors left because they couldn't afford insurance. Others say Hutchins isn't approving new tenants, letting the park wind down through attrition.

"He's 78 years old," Rafferty said. "Maybe he just wants to sell and be done with it. I can't blame him. But I wish somebody would tell us what's happening."

No clear path forward

Florida law offers limited protections for mobile home park residents. The Florida Mobile Home Act requires owners to give 12 months' notice before closing a park, and to provide relocation assistance of up to $3,000 per home. For residents of Camp Gulf, relocation would likely mean leaving Pensacola Beach entirely. No other mobile home parks exist on the island, and the nearest affordable options are in Pensacola proper, across the three-mile bridge.

For many, that bridge might as well be an ocean.

"I moved here to be near the water," Odom said. "I'm not going to spend my last years in some park off Nine Mile Road listening to traffic. I'd rather take my chances with the hurricanes."

The Escambia County Commission will take up the Camp Gulf lease at its October 15 meeting. Public comment will be accepted. As of this week, no agenda item has been posted.

The afternoon storm arrives on schedule, pushing through Camp Gulf with fat raindrops that steam on the hot pavement. Rafferty retreats inside his trailer. Through the screen door, the sound of a weather radio. The all-clear comes 20 minutes later. By then the sun is out again, and the wind sock has begun to stir.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 150,000 visitors and a transportation problem nobody solved
articles.dek: With the July show days away, Pensacola Beach road closures and parking plans remain unchanged from last year's gridlock. Local businesses are already bracing for complaints.
brief: The Blue Angels homecoming air show expects 150,000 visitors July 17-18, but Escambia County has made no significant changes to the transportation plan that caused hours-long traffic backups last year.
Pensacola Beach businesses report receiving calls from tourists asking about parking alternatives after last year's gridlock left some visitors stuck in traffic for three hours.
County officials say the Bob Sikes Bridge remains the bottleneck, but proposals for shuttle services from the mainland have stalled over funding and liability concerns.
articles.body:
The parking lot at Flounders Beach Cafe fills up by 7 a.m. during Blue Angels week. By 9, cars circle the lot like pelicans working a bait ball. By 11, the Bob Sikes Bridge becomes a mile-long parking lot, and the complaints start rolling in.

That was the scene last July. Business owners on Pensacola Beach say they have no reason to expect anything different this year.

"We're already getting calls," said Marcus Webb, general manager at a Via de Luna restaurant who asked that his employer not be named. "People want to know if there's a secret. There isn't. Get here early or don't come."

The Blue Angels homecoming air show, scheduled for July 17-18 at Pensacola Beach, is projected to draw 150,000 visitors across the two-day event, according to Visit Pensacola estimates. The economic impact runs into the tens of millions. Hotels from Perdido Key to Gulf Breeze have been booked for months.

What hasn't changed is the plan for getting all those people onto a barrier island accessible by a single two-lane bridge.

The bridge problem

The Bob Sikes Bridge, which connects Gulf Breeze to Pensacola Beach, handles roughly 15,000 vehicles on a normal summer Saturday. During the 2025 homecoming show, Escambia County estimated more than 35,000 vehicles attempted the crossing on Saturday alone.

Traffic backed up past the Tiger Point intersection in Gulf Breeze. Some visitors reported sitting in traffic for more than three hours. Social media posts showed families eating fast food in their cars, children sleeping in backseats, and at least one fender bender that further slowed the crawl.

"It was a mess," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach. "Nobody's pretending it wasn't."

But when asked what changes the county has implemented for 2026, Bergosh pointed to the same measures used last year: extended parking lot hours, additional portable restrooms, and sheriff's deputies directing traffic at key intersections.

"The bridge is the bridge," he said. "We can't add lanes in a year."

Shuttle proposals stall

For at least three years, various proposals have circulated for a mainland shuttle system that would reduce vehicle traffic on the bridge. Visitors would park at locations in Gulf Breeze or Pensacola and ride buses to the beach.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority discussed the concept at its February meeting. Escambia County staff presented a preliminary plan at a March workshop. Neither advanced to implementation.

According to county documents obtained by The Flightline through a public records request, the primary obstacles are funding and liability. A shuttle system would require leasing buses, hiring drivers, securing mainland parking locations, and obtaining insurance coverage for the temporary transit operation.

Estimated cost: between $180,000 and $340,000 for the two-day event, depending on scale.

"The question is who pays," said county spokesperson Angie Kinsella. "The event doesn't charge admission. There's no ticket revenue to offset costs."

Visit Pensacola, the tourism marketing organization funded by bed tax revenue, declined to comment on whether it had been approached about funding a shuttle system. A spokesperson said only that the organization "supports all efforts to improve the visitor experience."

Businesses brace

For restaurants and shops on Pensacola Beach, the air show is a double-edged sword. The crowds guarantee revenue. The gridlock guarantees frustration.

"Last year we had a table walk out because their parking meter expired and they couldn't get back to their car," said one restaurant manager on Via de Luna. "They'd been waiting 45 minutes for food. They just left."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority adjusted parking meter enforcement last year, extending free parking hours and suspending some time limits. Similar accommodations are planned for 2026.

But the core problem remains. Pensacola Beach has roughly 3,500 public parking spaces. On homecoming Saturday, demand exceeds 10,000.

Some visitors have found workarounds. Fishing charter captains report receiving calls about water taxi service from Pensacola or Gulf Breeze marinas. At least two operators ran unofficial shuttle boats last year, though none have announced plans for 2026.

"I'm not trying to become a ferry service," said one charter captain at Pensacola Beach Marina who declined to be named. "But people were offering me $200 to get them across the sound. That's hard to say no to."

No changes coming

With the show six days away, county officials confirm no significant changes to the 2026 transportation plan. The same parking lots will open at the same times. The same traffic pattern will direct vehicles onto and off the island. The same deputies will stand at the same intersections.

Bergosh said the county is "open to ideas" for future years but acknowledged nothing will change for this event.

"We tell people: come early, stay late, be patient," he said. "That's really all we can do."

For visitors already booked into hotels and vacation rentals, the advice may come too late. For business owners who will spend the weekend apologizing for traffic they can't control, it's become an annual ritual.

Webb, the restaurant manager, put it simply: "The jets are incredible. Getting here to see them is the price you pay."

The Blue Angels homecoming show runs Friday, July 17 and Saturday, July 18. Practice sessions are scheduled for July 14-16, typically drawing smaller crowds. Gates open at 8 a.m. both show days. The demonstration begins at 2 p.m.
